sources.title: DIVERSITY IS ALL YOU NEED : LEARNING SKILLS WITHOUT A REWARD FUNCTION

sectionsRead: Abstract; Sections 1–2: Introduction and Related Work
Sections 4.1–4.2.3: Skill analysis, initialization, hierarchical RL, imitation
Appendix C.1–C.2: Experimental details and environments
Appendix D.1–D.4: Training objectives, entropy, reward distributions, exploration
Appendix E.1–E.2: Learning the skill prior
Appendix F.1–F.2: Classic control and simulated robot skills

Separate supplemental material availability has not been fully verified.
PDF p. 20 was visually checked during source acquisition and contains only Figure 20 plus its extracted caption; figure images are not supplied to the text-only reading pass.

The preceding acquisition omissions are preserved. This reading additionally inspected all 22 supplied PDF pages, including Figure 20, and all six final original crops. All six text chunks were read individually; no supplied main-text or appendix section was omitted.

Identity/version: the title and four authors match the catalog work. The inspected artifact is arXiv:1802.06070v6, 9 October 2018, not an asserted byte-identical copy of the catalog's ICLR 2019 proceedings edition. The catalog BibTeX orders Ibarz before Gupta; the inspected title page orders Gupta before Ibarz.
Linked code, videos, external references and any separate supplements were not inspected; no experiments were reproduced.

synopsis: DIAYN learns a repertoire of stochastic, state-feedback skills without an external task reward. A discriminator rewards states that reveal which skill generated them, while action entropy and a fixed skill prior discourage narrow behavior and neglected skills. The repertoire supports reward-based adaptation, hierarchical control and state-only imitation, but task usefulness depends on what states become distinguishable (e-objective, e-loop, e-transfer, e-hierarchy, e-imitation).

problem.text: Sparse rewards and expensive human feedback make task-specific exploration difficult. The paper asks whether an agent can first interact without knowing its eventual reward, acquiring reusable behaviors that reduce later learning effort. This assumes access to environment interaction; it removes external reward supervision during pretraining, not the need for an optimization signal.

contributions.text: A variational information objective combines state–skill discriminability with stochastic control. A fixed categorical prior prevents early successful skills from monopolizing training.

The authors demonstrate emergent locomotion and three downstream uses: policy initialization, temporal composition and retrieval for imitation. These are simulated control experiments, not physical robot deployment.

inputs: Current environment state s and categorical skill z
Environment transitions during training; optional downstream task reward or expert state trajectory
outputs: A skill-conditioned stochastic action policy πθ(a | s, z)
A discriminator qφ(z | s), also usable for selecting an imitation skill

steps.name: Sample a skill and execute it
steps.detail: Draw z from a fixed uniform categorical prior at the beginning of an episode. Concatenate z with the current state for the policy, Q function and value function. Sample an action, execute it in the environment and observe the next state; the environment transition is not a learned world-model prediction.

steps.name: Turn classification into intrinsic reward
steps.detail: Train the discriminator to infer the sampled skill from individual visited states. Algorithm 1 evaluates the resulting next state and assigns log qφ(z | sₜ₊₁) − log p(z). The policy and discriminator cooperate: both benefit when the generated states identify the skill.

steps.name: Preserve stochasticity and sampling coverage
steps.detail: SAC maximizes the intrinsic return plus action entropy. Random actions must remain compatible with state discriminability, encouraging broader yet distinguishable behavior. A uniform prior keeps every skill eligible for training. State overlap is allowed when shared transitions eventually reach distinguishable regions.

training.text: The main implementation uses entropy coefficient α = 0.1. Appendix C specifies 300 hidden units for policy, Q and value networks, rather than the referenced SAC implementation's 128, and episodes of at most 1,000 steps. Other SAC hyperparameters are inherited by citation, not fully restated.

The pseudo-reward baseline affects termination incentives. Appendix A motivates retaining −log p(z) to discourage early termination, under its better-than-chance discriminator assumption; its footnote allows removal when rapid termination is desirable. This is a task-dependent choice, not a universal nonnegativity guarantee.

inference.text: For direct execution, fix z and repeatedly map the observed state to an action. For fine-tuning, evaluate skills with the task reward, select the best and initialize both policy and value networks before reward-based learning.

A downstream meta-controller chooses skills for k steps: k = 10 for cheetah hurdles and 100 for ant navigation. The low-level policy still uses state feedback within each interval. The ant DIAYN+prior variant supplies the discriminator with center-of-mass information.

For imitation from states without expert actions, enumerate skills and choose the one maximizing the product of discriminator probabilities along the demonstration. Execute that existing feedback policy; no inverse-dynamics model is trained and no new skill is synthesized.

equations.explanation: S, A and Z denote states, actions and the skill variable; I is mutual information and H entropy, using natural logarithms. The fixed uniform prior maximizes skill entropy, state classification reduces conditional skill uncertainty, and the final term preserves action randomness.

The learned discriminator qφ approximates the unavailable posterior p(z | s); θ and φ are policy and discriminator parameters. The expectation uses states visited under the skill. SAC implements the entropy term with coefficient α. Equation 3 defines the bracketed quantity as pseudo-reward.

results.setting: Modified HalfCheetah-v1 with repeated hurdles; meta-controller selects a skill every 10 steps.
results.metric: Task reward versus training hours; higher is better
results.value: Approximately 4–4.5 reward near 9 hours, read from the solid DIAYN curve in Figure 7.
results.comparison: TRPO and VIME fluctuate substantially lower, roughly around 1–2 over this interval; SAC remains near zero.
results.interpretation: Graph-read estimates, not tabulated scores. The dashed DIAYN continuation is not treated as additional measured samples; uncertainty and seed aggregation are not specified for this plot.

results.setting: Modified Ant-v1; five ordered waypoint rewards, maximum +5; k = 100.
results.metric: Accumulated waypoint reward; higher is better
results.value: DIAYN+prior reaches approximately 2.2–2.4 near 15 hours; plain DIAYN is roughly 0.4–0.5.
results.comparison: The added center-of-mass prior accounts for the pronounced separation from plain DIAYN, TRPO, VIME and SAC.
results.interpretation: Approximate Figure 7 readings do not establish reliable completion of all five waypoints. The stronger variant includes task-relevant prior knowledge.

results.setting: Half-cheetah, hopper and ant; best pretrained skill versus random initialization, same architecture; five-seed averages.
results.metric: Benchmark reward versus downstream training hours
results.value: Figure 5 shows faster early learning with DIAYN initialization in all three environments; exact endpoint values are not tabulated.
results.comparison: Both policy and value networks are initialized from pretraining; the baseline starts from scratch.
results.interpretation: Pretraining cost is explicitly omitted under a free-or-amortized-pretraining assumption. This does not demonstrate lower total interaction or compute cost.

results.setting: Inverted pendulum and mountain car; three seeds per environment in Figure 17; fixed versus learned prior.
results.metric: Effective sampled skills, exp(H[Z]); higher indicates broader sampling
results.value: Fixed uniform sampling retains 50 effective skills; learned-prior curves fall to roughly 1–3 late in training.
results.comparison: Appendix E reports an order-of-magnitude reduction; the half-cheetah comparison appears separately in Figure 4.
results.interpretation: This measures sampling entropy, not independently verified behavioral diversity. The VIC-labeled comparator is implemented by learning the prior within DIAYN.

results.setting: 600 synthetic imitation tasks using expert trajectories from another DIAYN seed; classic-control evaluation.
results.metric: L2 trajectory distance versus discriminator log score; lower distance is better
results.value: Figure 22 shows generally lower distances for DIAYN; curves approach the low-entropy variant at high scores. No aggregate numerical error is tabulated.
results.comparison: Lower entropy, learned prior, and five skills instead of 50; qualitative half-cheetah examples succeed on three of four demonstrations.
results.interpretation: Synthetic expert generation limits generalization claims. The handstand fails; score–distance association is not calibrated execution-safety evidence.

limitations.text: Discriminability need not match downstream usefulness. Ant skills often follow arcs rather than running straight; Figure 15 reports no learned skill above 1,000 on that benchmark. More entropy broadens exploration but excessive entropy makes skills harder to distinguish.

Section 3.3 claims a unique evenly partitioned gridworld optimum, but Appendix B proves an unregularized two-skill optimum and only near-optimality with entropy, under exact stationary visitation. It supplies neither the stated uniqueness guarantee nor continuous-control convergence.

Source notation is inconsistent: Section 3.1 names state–skill information but prints I(A;Z), whereas Equation 1 uses I(S;Z). Figure 1's feedback label uses sₜ while its discriminator block and Algorithm 1 use sₜ₊₁. The explanation follows Equation 1 and Algorithm 1.

reproduction.text: Reconstruct the listed Gym versions and custom tasks. Ant uses joint gear ratio 30, square-corner goals at coordinates ±2 m and a 0.5 m acceptance radius; hurdle boxes are 0.25 m high, 0.1 m wide and 1 m deep, spaced every 3 m. Match these before comparing curves.

Appendix C says 1,000 episodes per epoch but also equates 1,000 epochs with at most one million steps; Figure 5 instead labels time in hours. This accounting is unresolved. Hardware, complete discriminator configuration and exact baseline entropy settings are not supplied, so precise timing replication requires additional information.

reasoning.text: The catalog's foundational-policy placement and not-applicable world-action-model axes are supported. DIAYN learns an action policy and a state-to-skill discriminator; its environment transition is fixed. Neither joint future/action prediction nor inverse dynamics appears. Multiple learned components alone do not make this a world-model/action-model architecture.

discussionQuestions: Does fixing the prior improve behavioral coverage beyond the sampling entropy it guarantees? (e-prior)
When does center-of-mass supervision improve reusable skills rather than specializing them to one navigation task? (e-hierarchy)
How many downstream tasks are needed to amortize DIAYN pretraining? (e-transfer)

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title/author block and arXiv margin
evidence.detail: Title matches the observed manifest title. Authors, in order: Benjamin Eysenbach, Abhishek Gupta, Julian Ibarz, Sergey Levine. Affiliations shown are Carnegie Mellon University, UC Berkeley and Google Brain. Margin identifies arXiv:1802.06070v6, 9 Oct 2018.
Motivates reward-free skill acquisition for sparse rewards, expensive feedback and hierarchical reuse; describes subsequent reward-based applications.

Fixed prior and environment are green; policy and discriminator are learned blue blocks. Algorithm samples a skill per episode, executes actions, scores next states, updates policy with SAC and discriminator with SGD. Diagram feedback label uses s_t despite s_{t+1} in its block and algorithm.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 3–4, Sections 3.1–3.3, Equations 1–3 and variational bound
evidence.detail: Defines state–skill mutual information, action entropy and conditional action–skill penalty; uses a discriminator lower bound, uniform categorical prior, SAC and intrinsic log-posterior-minus-log-prior reward. Section 3.1's I(A;Z) notation conflicts with its prose and Equation 1.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Section 3.2; p. 14, Appendix C opening paragraph and C.1
evidence.detail: Sets α = 0.1; specifies 300 hidden units for policy/Q/value, concatenated skill inputs, maximum 1,000-step episodes, inherited SAC settings and Gym environment versions. Epoch/episode/step statements are internally inconsistent; full hardware and discriminator configuration are absent.

evidence.location: PDF p. 12, Appendix A and footnote 5
evidence.detail: Motivates the log-prior baseline using absorbing states and survival incentives, under a better-than-chance assumption; permits removal for tasks favoring early termination.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Section 3.3; pp. 12–13, Appendix B, Lemmas B.1–B.2 and Figures 10–11
evidence.detail: Main text states uniqueness. Appendix assumes exact stationary visitation, constructs an unregularized two-skill optimum and states an entropy-regularized gap of log(4)/(2N), with N the grid side length; it discusses short borders and bottlenecks.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Figure 2b; p. 6, Section 4.1, Question 3
evidence.detail: Skills share a hallway then separate in a room; cumulative return allows temporarily indistinguishable states.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Figure 3 and Question 1; p. 16, Appendix D.3–D.4 and Figure 15; pp. 18–21, Appendix F and Figures 18–21
evidence.detail: Shows diverse simulated locomotion and classic-control behaviors. Ant often moves in arcs; Appendix D.3 states no learned ant skill exceeds 1,000 benchmark reward. Figures 19–21 depict additional half-cheetah, hopper and ant skills.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Figure 5 and Section 4.2.1; p. 7, opening paragraph
evidence.detail: Five-seed average curves compare reward versus hours for DIAYN and random initialization. The highest-reward skill initializes both policy and value networks. Pretraining steps are excluded because pretraining is assumed free or amortized.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Section 4.2.2, Figures 6–7; p. 8, Question 7
evidence.detail: Meta-controller chooses skills every 10 cheetah or 100 ant steps. Figure 7 solid cheetah DIAYN curve approaches 4–4.5 near 9 hours; ant DIAYN+prior is about 2.2–2.4 near 15 hours and plain DIAYN about 0.4–0.5. Center-of-mass discriminator input supplies the additional prior. Figure 6 uses 25 goals and five seeds.

Lists Gym versions, hurdle geometry and ant modifications. Ant gear ratio is 30, ordered square-corner goals are at ±2 m, acceptance radius is 0.5 m and rewards sum to at most +5. Point navigation uses squared-distance goal reward and can be solved by choosing one skill.

evidence.location: PDF p. 15, Appendix D.2, unnumbered three-panel sweep; p. 16, first paragraph
evidence.detail: For a point mass controlling orientation and forward velocity, compares α = 0.01, 1 and 10. Low entropy produces narrow trajectories; more entropy broadens coverage; very high entropy makes skills harder to distinguish. No coverage statistic or uncertainty is reported for this sweep.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Figure 4 and Question 4; pp. 17–18, Appendix E.1–E.2 and Figure 17
evidence.detail: VIC-labeled comparison learns the prior within DIAYN using p(z) proportional to exp of expected discriminator log score. Fixed prior gives 50 effective skills. Figure 17 shows three learned-prior seeds per classic-control task approaching roughly 1–3 effective skills; Figure 4 separately shows half-cheetah. Effective count is exp(H[Z]).

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Section 4.2.3 and Figure 9; p. 22, Appendix G–G.1, Equation 5 and Figure 22
evidence.detail: Enumerates skills by product of state discriminator scores; relates retrieval to an M-projection under a perfect discriminator and fixed prior. Figure 9 shows three successes and failed handstand. Figure 22 aggregates 600 synthetic tasks from another seed; baseline variants lower entropy, learn the prior, or use five instead of 50 skills. Distance is L2 in state space; no aggregate numerical error or calibrated safety test is given.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 3–8 and 12–22, method and experiment figures throughout the main text and appendices
evidence.detail: The supplied paper presents its quantitative evidence in plots and its method in Figure 1 with Algorithm 1. It contains no numerical results table; entropy and prior comparisons are graphical diagnostics.
